You can also open the position yourself. That final case is different: Manual Bot may adopt it, but Manual Bot never creates the entry. Hedge Bot is different again; it waits until a main position already exists. A valid signal is not automatically an order. Wick Hunter checks the selected market, direction, pair scope, blacklists, per-bot deal limits, and account-level exposure controls. Imagine a bot that allows two longs, two shorts, but only three deals combined. Two longs plus one short uses the full combined allowance, so the next signal is skipped even though one short slot still appears available. These gates refuse new exposure; they do not close an existing position or erase its protection. Activity records the first rule that blocked the attempt.

When the gates pass, the selected execution method sends the entry. A deal slot is reserved while the order is still being placed, so several simultaneous signals cannot slip through a limit. After the exchange confirms the position, Wick Hunter assigns its owner. Ownership matters because one manager should control the main position's DCA ladder, take profit, stop, history, and P and L attribution. A pending or uncertain order can temporarily retain that claim until the app proves what happened, preventing a second bot from taking over the same exposure. The DCA ladder adds exposure only at the saved distances and sizes. Here is an illustrative long: one thousand dollars opens at one hundred dollars, then a five-hundred-dollar DCA fills at ninety-five.

The combined average moves to about ninety-eight dollars and twenty-eight cents. A one-percent take-profit target therefore moves from one hundred one to roughly ninety-nine twenty-six. The ladder's distance plan remains anchored to the original entry, while the take profit follows the changing average. A deeper ladder can improve the recovery price, but it also commits more capital and increases risk. Take profit is normally a reduce-only order on the exchange. It is recalculated after a DCA or manual size change so both its price and quantity match the live position. Where the venue supports it, Wick Hunter also rests a real reduce-only stop order on the exchange. If the venue or position cannot support that order, the deal clearly identifies a monitored fallback that requires the app and a live price.

A value of zero turns that protection off. These exits manage risk, but they cannot guarantee the price received during a fast market. Hedge Bot never opens the main position. It may attach afterward, when the exchange, market, pair, and bot settings support it. The main owner stays responsible for the original position, while Hedge Bot owns measured opposite-side coverage in separate tranches. During an active attachment, the hedge workflow can coordinate both legs and their combined exit. For example, a one-thousand-dollar main long with forty-percent coverage holds roughly four hundred dollars short. That can reduce directional exposure, but it also adds orders, fees, funding, and configuration risk. At the exit, Wick Hunter closes or reduces the intended position, cancels remaining ladder orders, and keeps the pair claimed until cleanup is confirmed.

It then reconciles the result against information published by the exchange. Deals tells you what is still open. Activity explains entries, skips, changes, fills, and cleanup. P and L attributes the settled result to the owning bot, including available fees and funding. The full workflow is visible, but visibility does not remove trading risk. Start small, verify the exchange, and confirm that every live position has the protection you expect.

title: Connect Bybit Securely | Wick Hunter Course 2
recordedVersion: September 2026 recording; current written guide takes precedence

chunks.text: This lesson connects a Bybit account to Wick Hunter with a restricted API key. The key needs permission to read the account and place trading orders. It never needs permission to withdraw or transfer funds. Keeping those permissions disabled preserves the non-custodial boundary, even if a trading key is ever exposed. In Bybit, open Account Settings, choose API, and select Create New Key. Choose API Transaction and give the key a recognizable name. Select Read-Write, because a read-only key can display balances and positions but cannot place, change, or close orders. When available, restrict the key to your Wick Hunter server's public IP address. Enable only the trading scope required by the markets you will connect. Contract trading permission is required for futures.

Add spot trading only if you intend to use supported spot functionality. Leave Assets, Account Transfer, Subaccount Transfer, Convert, and Withdrawal completely disabled. Wick Hunter has no feature that needs to move funds out of your account. Never enable an entire permission group merely because it is faster. Bybit may request a security verification before creating the key. Complete that step privately, without recording verification codes or opening your inbox on screen. This tutorial skips the private verification process and resumes only after the key is created. Before continuing, confirm one final time that withdrawal and transfer permissions remain off. After creation, Bybit displays the API key and secret. The secret is shown only once.

Copy both values directly into Wick Hunter; do not store them in notes, screenshots, recordings, chat, or source code. If either value appears in a recording or is shared accidentally, treat that key as compromised: revoke it immediately and create a replacement. In Wick Hunter, open Accounts and choose Add Account. Select Bybit, add a label you will recognize, and paste the API key and secret into their matching fields. Select only the markets covered by the key's trading permissions. For perpetual futures, choose Hedge Mode so Wick Hunter can manage independent long and short legs when the strategy requires them. Choose Add Account and let Wick Hunter validate each selected market. It checks the credentials, trading scopes, and position mode without placing a test order.

A read-only key or missing market permission is refused instead of being presented as ready. Confirm the account card shows the expected market and an active connection before enabling any bot. Keep withdrawals disabled for the entire life of the key.

title: What Is Wick Hunter Unleashed? | Course 1
recordedVersion: September 2026 recording; current written guide takes precedence

chunks.text: Wick Hunter Unleashed is an automated trade-management platform. It connects an exchange account to a collection of specialized bots, then gives those bots one shared system for position sizing, dollar-cost averaging, take profit, stop protection, monitoring, and profit attribution. The goal is not to predict every market move. The goal is to apply a strategy consistently, enforce its limits before new exposure is opened, and keep each managed position visible from entry through cleanup. Throughout this course, all figures are illustrative rather than recommended settings, and automation never removes trading risk. The Dashboard is the operational overview. Wallet and equity show the account snapshot. Day P and L shows the result recorded for the current UTC day.

Open Deals tells you how many positions Wick Hunter is managing, including any with Hedge Bot coverage. Bots Running confirms how much automation is enabled, and the equity chart shows how the account changed over time. For example, an illustrative dashboard might show ten-thousand-five dollars of equity, two bots running, and three open deals. That does not tell you whether those deals are safe. It tells you where to begin the review. Different bots answer different entry questions. Liq Scalper looks for qualifying forced liquidations beyond a fixed VWMA band. Optimized Liquidation Bot computes a separate band for every pair. TV Signal lets a TradingView alert request the entry. Manual Bot adopts an eligible position you opened yourself; it never creates the entry.

Hedge Bot is different again. It waits until a main position already exists, then may build measured opposite-side coverage. For example, TV Signal can open a long after an alert, the shared deal engine can place its ladder and exits, and Hedge Bot may attach afterward if that account, market, pair, and configuration support it. Before a new position is opened, Wick Hunter applies the bot's scope and the account's risk gates. It checks the selected account and market, allowed direction, pair list and exclusions, bot deal limits, account exposure limits, and whether another manager already owns that symbol. Suppose Max Longs is two, Max Shorts is two, and Max Both is three. Two longs plus one short fill the combined limit, so another short signal is skipped even though its side still appears to have one slot.

Activity records the reason. These rules block new exposure; they do not silently close a position already being managed. Once an entry becomes a live position, one bot owns the main deal. That owner coordinates its DCA ladder, take profit, stop protection, history, and P and L attribution. Imagine a one-thousand-dollar long at one hundred dollars, followed by a five-hundred-dollar DCA at ninety-five. The combined average moves to roughly ninety-eight dollars and twenty-eight cents, so a one-percent take-profit target moves to about ninety-nine dollars and twenty-six cents. The ladder can improve the recovery price, but it also adds size and risk. If Hedge Bot attaches, it owns only the separate opposite-side hedge tranches; the main owner does not change.

The platform separates four useful questions. My Bots shows what automation exists and whether it is enabled. Deals shows live positions and their protection. Activity explains entries, skips, order changes, fills, and cleanup. P and L shows settled exchange results attributed to the owning bot, including available fees and funding. For example, a BTC signal refused by a pair blacklist appears in Activity but never becomes a Deal. A position that closes later disappears from Deals and becomes part of P and L. This separation makes a quiet bot easier to diagnose without guessing that every empty screen is a failure. The course now moves from foundation to operation. First, connect a restricted exchange API key with withdrawal and transfer permissions disabled.

Next, learn the trade lifecycle and the differences among the five supported bot types. Then study the detailed settings tutorials before choosing values. Finally, use Deals and Activity to verify that each live position has the orders and protection you expect. A practical learning sequence is one account, one bot, and one very small position, followed by a complete review of entry, ladder, take profit, stop, and ownership. Wick Hunter organizes automation, but you remain responsible for configuration, supervision, and market risk.
